content: Chlorphenamine is an antihistamine medication that is approved by the FDA for the treatment of allergic rhinitis and the common cold. It is commonly associated with side effects such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness. Adult Dosage and Indications: 1. FDA-Approved Dosage for Allergies: For 4-hour allergy tablets: Take 1 tablet (4 mg) every 4 to 6 hours, with a maximum of 6 tablets in 24 hours. For 8-hour allergy tablets: Take 1 tablet (8 mg) every 8 to 12 hours, with a maximum of 3 tablets in 24 hours. For 12-hour tablets: Take 1 tablet (12 mg) every 12 hours, with a maximum of 2 tablets in 24 hours. To prevent allergic rhinitis symptoms, start with 4 mg (syrup or plain tablet) three times daily and gradually increase every 3 days as tolerated, up to 8 mg three times daily. Begin treatment before allergy season (e.g., August 1st for ragweed) and continue until the allergen is no longer present (e.g., first frost in ragweed areas). Patients often develop tolerance to the sedative effects if the dose is started low and increased incrementally. 2. Dosage for Cough: Administer 2 teaspoonfuls of Codeprex™ (10 mL, equivalent to codeine 40 mg and chlorpheniramine maleate 8 mg) orally every 12 hours, with a maximum of 4 teaspoonfuls in 24 hours. Pediatric Dosage and Indications: 1. FDA-Approved Dosage for Children: Over-the-counter (OTC) cough and cold medications containing chlorpheniramine are not recommended for children under 2 years of age due to the risk of serious and potentially life-threatening effects. The FDA issued a public health advisory in January 2008 regarding this risk. Chlorpheniramine may cause excitability in children. The 8-hour and 12-hour allergy tablets are not recommended for children under 12 years, and the 4-hour allergy tablets are not recommended for children under 6 years. For children aged 6 to 11 years, the dose is half the adult dose: 2 mg (half of a 4 mg tablet) every 4 to 6 hours, with a maximum of 12 mg in 24 hours. For children aged 6 to 12 years with allergic rhinitis, start with 2 mg and increase progressively to a maximum of 12 mg per day. For children aged 6 to 12 years with cough, allergic rhinitis, or hay fever: Administer 1 teaspoonful of Codeprex™ (5 mL, equivalent to codeine 20 mg and chlorpheniramine maleate 4 mg) orally every 12 hours, with a maximum of 2 teaspoonfuls in 24 hours. For children aged 12 years and older with cough, allergic rhinitis, or hay fever: Administer 2 teaspoonfuls of Codeprex™ (10 mL, equivalent to codeine 40 mg and chlorpheniramine maleate 8 mg) orally every 12 hours, with a maximum of 4 teaspoonfuls in 24 hours. 2. Maximum Dosage for Children: The maximum recommended dose for oral chlorpheniramine in children aged 6 to 11 years is 12 mg per day. Contraindications: Chlorpheniramine is contraindicated in individuals with hypersensitivity to chlorpheniramine or dexchlorpheniramine. Warnings: Consult a healthcare provider before use if you have breathing problems such as emphysema or chronic bronchitis, glaucoma, or difficulty urinating due to an enlarged prostate gland. Consult a doctor or pharmacist before use if you are taking sedatives or tranquilizers. This medication may cause marked drowsiness. Avoid consuming alcohol, as it may increase drowsiness. Exercise caution when driving or operating machinery. Excitability may occur, particularly in children. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, consult a healthcare professional before use. Adverse Reactions: Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness. There is limited information available regarding adverse reactions from clinical trials or postmarketing data. Drug Interactions: Chlorpheniramine may interact with a variety of medications, including but not limited to: Almotriptan, amitriptyline, amoxapine, belladonna alkaloids, bupropion, desvenlafaxine, dolasetron, donepezil, fentanyl, fluoxetine, fosphenytoin, granisetron, hydroxytryptophan, levomilnacipran, lorcaserin, mepenzolate, meperidine, metoprolol, mirtazapine, morphine, palonosetron, phenytoin, procarbazine, tramadol, trazodone, umeclidinium, vilazodone, vortioxetine, and ziprasidone. Use in Specific Populations: 1. Pregnancy: There is no specific FDA or Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine during pregnancy. 2. Labor and Delivery: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine during labor and delivery. 3. Nursing Mothers: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine in breastfeeding mothers. 4. Pediatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine in pediatric patients beyond the dosing recommendations provided. 5. Geriatric Use: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine in elderly patients. 6. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 7. Immunocompromised Patients: There is no FDA guidance on the use of chlorpheniramine in immunocompromised patients. Administration and Monitoring: There is limited information available regarding the administration and monitoring of chlorpheniramine. Overdosage: In the event of suspected overdose, contact the National Poison Help hotline (1-800-222-1222) immediately. Pharmacology: There is limited information available regarding the mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of chlorpheniramine. Patient Counseling Information: Adults and children aged 12 years and older should take 1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding 6 doses in 24 hours. Children aged 6 to under 12 years should take half a tablet every 4 to 6 hours, not exceeding 6 doses in 24 hours. Children under 6 years should consult a doctor before use. Alcohol Precautions: The interaction between alcohol and chlorpheniramine has not been established. Consult a healthcare provider regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication. Brand Names: Chlorphenamine is marketed under various brand names, including Aller-Chlor, C P M, Chlor-Phen, Chlor-Trimeton Allergy, Chlorphen, Diabetic Tussin Allergy Relief, Efidac 24 Chlorpheniramine, and Teldrin HBP.
